summary.text: Take the composite number \(N=23492890653051=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341\).  The identity \(\sum_{k=1}^n\gcd(k,n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\varphi(n/d)\), together with multiplicativity and the prime value \(2p-1\), gives \(\sum_{k=1}^N\gcd(k,N)=26N-1\); hence the relevant gcd is \(\gcd(N,26N)=N\), so the quotient is \(1\) despite \(N\) being composite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd\!\left(n,\,1+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(k,n)\right)}.
\]
We will exhibit the composite positive integer
\[
N=23492890653051
\]
for which \(a(N)=1\). This disproves the claimed equivalence.

Define the gcd-sum
\[
S(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(k,n).
\]
We first derive a convenient formula for this sum. Replacing the term indexed by \(k=n\) with a term indexed by \(k=0\) does not change the sum, because
\(\gcd(n,n)=n=\gcd(n,0)\). Hence
\[
S(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\gcd(n,k).
\]
Group the integers \(k\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}\) according to the value
\(d=\gcd(n,k)\). Such a value \(d\) must divide \(n\). If \(d\mid n\), writing \(k=dj\) gives
\[
\gcd(n,k)=d
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\gcd(n/d,j)=1,
\]
with \(0\leq j<n/d\). There are exactly \(\varphi(n/d)\) such residue classes \(j\), where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function. (This also handles \(d=n\): then \(n/d=1\), and the single value \(j=0\) is counted by \(\varphi(1)=1\).) Consequently,
\[
S(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\,\varphi(n/d). \tag{1}
\]

The arithmetic function on the right side of (1) is multiplicative. Indeed, suppose \(m\) and \(n\) are coprime. Every divisor of \(mn\) has a unique form \(ab\), where \(a\mid m\) and \(b\mid n\). Moreover, \(m/a\) and \(n/b\) are coprime, so the multiplicativity of Euler's totient gives
\[
\varphi\!\left(\frac{mn}{ab}\right)
 =\varphi(m/a)\varphi(n/b).
\]
Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(mn)
 &=\sum_{a\mid m}\sum_{b\mid n}ab\,
   \varphi(m/a)\varphi(n/b)\\
 &=\left(\sum_{a\mid m}a\varphi(m/a)\right)
   \left(\sum_{b\mid n}b\varphi(n/b)\right)\\
 &=S(m)S(n). \tag{2}
\end{aligned}
\]
For a prime \(p\), its only divisors are \(1\) and \(p\), and therefore (1) gives
\[
S(p)=\varphi(p)+p\varphi(1)=(p-1)+p=2p-1. \tag{3}
\]

The number \(N\) has the factorization
\[
N=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341. \tag{4}
\]
For completeness, all five factors in (4) are prime. The primality of the two larger factors can be established compactly by the following elementary form of Lucas's primality criterion: if the complete prime factorization of \(M-1\) is known and there is an integer \(c\) such that
\[
c^{M-1}\equiv1\pmod M
\]
and, for every prime \(q\mid M-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(c^{(M-1)/q}-1,M\bigr)=1,
\]
then \(M\) is prime. To see why, let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(M\). The order of \(c\) modulo \(r\) divides \(M-1\). The coprimality condition for each \(q\mid M-1\) says that this order does not divide \((M-1)/q\), so it contains the full power of every prime occurring in \(M-1\). Hence the order is divisible by \(M-1\). Since the order also divides \(r-1\), we have \(M-1\mid r-1\), and therefore \(r\ge M\). As \(r\mid M\), this forces \(r=M\), proving that \(M\) is prime.

For \(42307\), we have
\[
42307-1=42306=2\cdot3\cdot11\cdot641.
\]
The number \(641\) is prime: since \(25^2<641<26^2\), it is enough to test the primes at most \(25\), and the remainders of \(641\) modulo
\(2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\) are respectively
\[
1,2,1,4,3,4,12,14,20,
\]
all nonzero. Using \(c=3\), repeated squaring modulo \(42307\) gives
\[
3^{42306}\equiv1\pmod{42307},
\]
and the residues for the four prime divisors of \(42306\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&(42306)/q&3^{42306/q}\pmod{42307}\\ \hline
2&21153&42306\\
3&14102&36715\\
11&3846&17937\\
641&66&10961
\end{array}
\]
The required gcds are all \(1\). Explicitly, if \(r\) denotes the residue in the last column, the following Bézout identities give
\(x(r-1)+y\cdot42307=1\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r}
q&x&y\\ \hline
2&21153&-21152\\
3&-12239&10621\\
11&6088&-2581\\
641&-6651&1723
\end{array}
\]
Thus the criterion proves that \(42307\) is prime.

Similarly,
\[
116341-1=116340=2^2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot277.
\]
The number \(277\) is prime: \(16^2<277<17^2\), and its remainders modulo the primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) are
\[
1,1,2,4,2,4,
\]
all nonzero. With \(c=14\), repeated squaring modulo \(116341\) gives
\[
14^{116340}\equiv1\pmod{116341},
\]
and
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&116340/q&14^{116340/q}\pmod{116341}\\ \hline
2&58170&116340\\
3&38780&50801\\
5&23268&81650\\
7&16620&10889\\
277&420&35125
\end{array}
\]
Again the coprimality conditions follow from explicit Bézout identities. For each row, with \(r\) the residue in the last column, the displayed \(x,y\) satisfy
\(x(r-1)+y\cdot116341=1\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r}
q&x&y\\ \hline
2&58170&-58169\\
3&21846&-9539\\
5&-15490&10871\\
7&-9200&861\\
277&-9026&2725
\end{array}
\]
Therefore \(116341\) is prime as well.

The remaining primality checks are immediate trial divisions. The numbers \(3\), \(37\), and \(43\) have no prime divisor at most their respective square roots: for \(37\), the remainders modulo \(2,3,5\) are \(1,1,2\), and for \(43\) they are \(1,1,3\). Thus all factors in (4) are distinct primes and hence pairwise coprime. The multiplication in (4) can also be checked through the partial products
\[
3\cdot37=111,
\quad111\cdot43=4773,
\quad4773\cdot42307=201931311,
\]
\[
201931311\cdot116341=23492890653051=N.
\]

We may now use multiplicativity (2) and the prime evaluation (3). For the five primes in (4), the values \(2p-1\) are
\[
5,\quad73,\quad85,\quad84613,\quad232681.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(N)
 &=5\cdot73\cdot85\cdot84613\cdot232681\\
 &=610815156979325.
\end{aligned}
\]
For transparency, the partial products are
\[
5\cdot73=365,
\quad365\cdot85=31025,
\quad31025\cdot84613=2625118325,
\]
\[
2625118325\cdot232681=610815156979325.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
26N=26\cdot23492890653051=610815156979326.
\]
Therefore
\[
S(N)=26N-1. \tag{5}
\]
It follows from (5) that
\[
1+S(N)=26N.
\]
Since \(N\mid26N\),
\[
\gcd(N,1+S(N))=\gcd(N,26N)=N.
\]
Hence
\[
a(N)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,1+S(N))}=\frac NN=1. \tag{6}
\]

Finally, \(N\) is neither \(1\) nor prime. Indeed,
\[
N=3\cdot7830963551017,
\]
where both factors are greater than \(1\). Thus \(N\) is composite. Equation (6) supplies a composite positive integer for which \(a(N)=1\), contradicting the proposed assertion that \(a(n)=1\) occurs only when \(n=1\) or \(n\) is prime. Therefore the conjecture is false.
